lesson.title: Keep every atom

lead.text: In a chemical reaction, substances change into other substances. A candle flame turns wax and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water vapour, and iron rusts when it meets oxygen and moisture. The atoms in the starting substances are rearranged into the new ones. No atom is created or destroyed on the way.

An equation records this. The starting substances, called reactants, go on the left and the substances made, called products, go on the right, with an arrow between. Sodium burns in chlorine gas to make sodium chloride, and the equation is 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl. The numbers in front are coefficients, as in the lesson on reading formulas. They say how many of each unit take part.

Count the atoms on each side. The left has 2 Na atoms and 2 Cl atoms, and the 2 NaCl units on the right hold the same. When every element has the same count on both sides, the equation is called a balanced equation. If the counts differ, atoms have appeared or vanished somewhere and the equation is wrong.
Lithium reacts with fluorine gas to make lithium fluoride. A coefficient multiplies every atom in its formula.

Most equations start unbalanced. Hydrogen and chlorine make hydrogen chloride. Written with one of each, H₂ + Cl₂ → HCl, it has 2 H atoms and 2 Cl atoms on the left and 1 H atom and 1 Cl atom on the right. Atoms have vanished, so something is wrong.

Fix it by changing a coefficient. Two HCl units hold 2 H atoms and 2 Cl atoms, so H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl is balanced. The method is to count each element on both sides and look for one that does not match. Change a coefficient until it does, and then count everything again, because a coefficient multiplies every element in its formula.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows magnesium burning in oxygen. With one of each, the oxygen on the right falls short. With two MgO the oxygen matches, and now the magnesium does not. Use the coefficient buttons to try other values and watch the counts below the drawing. Fixing one element can upset another, which is why you count everything again after each change.

lead.text: When a count refuses to match, there is a tempting shortcut, which is to change a subscript. Suppose an equation needs one more oxygen atom on the right. Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ would supply it. But H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance, and the equation would then describe a reaction that never happens.
A coefficient is safe because it only changes how many molecules there are. 2 H₂O is two molecules of water, and each is still water. So the formulas stay fixed and only the coefficients change.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the same idea for making water. Changing the coefficient of H₂O changes how many water molecules there are, and the hydrogen and oxygen counts change with it. Each molecule is still H₂O, whichever case you pick.

lead.text: Count the oxygen atoms in the product first, then ask how many O₂ molecules supply them.

reveal.text: You matched oxygen on both sides by working out how many O₂ molecules supply those atoms. That is balancing.

steps.headline: Balance ? K + Cl₂ → 2 KCl. What goes before K?

workedSteps.text: Count chlorine. The product has 2 Cl, and Cl₂ on the left has 2.
Count potassium. The product has 2 K, so the left needs 2.
Write the coefficient in front of K. Never touch the subscripts.

steps.headline: Balance CH₄ + ? O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. What goes before O₂?

workedSteps.text: Count oxygen on the right: 2 in CO₂ and 2 in the waters.
Find how many O₂ molecules supply that many O atoms.

lead.text: A longer equation needs a plan, because each coefficient affects several counts. A good plan is to begin with an element that appears in just one substance on each side, and to leave an element that stands alone, such as O₂, until last. A lone element can be adjusted without upsetting anything else.

Burning propane, C₃H₈, the fuel in camping stoves, shows the order. Carbon and hydrogen each appear once on each side, so they go first: 3 CO₂ matches the 3 carbon atoms and 4 H₂O matches the 8 hydrogen atoms. Oxygen comes last because it appears in two products. Add up the oxygen in the products: 3 CO₂ hold 6 atoms and 4 H₂O hold 4, so there are 10 in all. Each O₂ supplies 2, which makes 5 O₂. The finished equation is C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O.
Count each element on the right first, then match the left.
Ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen. Balance the hydrogen by counting the atoms in the ammonia.

lesson.orientation: Balance reactions by changing coefficients while preserving chemical formulas.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A toy factory builds cars, and every car needs 4 wheels. The wheels arrive in packs of 2. An order comes in for 3 cars. Three cars need 3 × 4 = 12 wheels, and 12 wheels come from 6 packs. Open five packs and the last car is short. Open seven and there are wheels left over on the floor.

A chemical reaction follows the same rule. The last lesson showed how to count and weigh a sample. In a reaction the atoms are rearranged into new substances, and the factory has no spare parts: every atom that goes in has to come out again somewhere. Writing a reaction down is like writing an order for molecules, and the order has to use exactly the atoms available.
This lesson works out how many of each molecule an order needs, so that no atom is lost and none appears from nowhere.

intro.promise: By the end you'll balance a simple reaction by choosing coefficients so that every atom is accounted for.
intro.whyItMatters: A balanced equation is the starting point for every calculation about a reaction.

recap.keyIdea: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. You balance by changing coefficients, never subscripts.

blocks.text: Back on the factory floor, the wheels were the atoms and the packs were the molecules. You balanced the O₂ for water and for methane, and the H₂ for ammonia. Each time you counted one element at a time and adjusted a coefficient.

recap.nextHook: A balanced equation is also a recipe. The next lesson reads its coefficients as ratios between amounts and uses them to say how much of one substance goes with another.

questions.prompt: Balance 2 H₂ + ? O₂ → 2 H₂O. What coefficient belongs before O₂?
hints: Count oxygen atoms on both sides.
Two waters contain two oxygen atoms.
Divide the two required O atoms by two atoms per O₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two waters contain two O atoms, supplied by one O₂.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Two waters contain two O atoms, and one O₂ supplies exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: Two O₂ would supply four O atoms, but the two waters hold only two.

questions.prompt: Balance CH₄ + ? O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. What coefficient belongs before O₂?
hints: Include the oxygen inside water.
CO₂ has two O atoms and two waters have two more.
Divide the total four O atoms by two per O₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products contain four O atoms, so two O₂ molecules are needed.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The products hold four O atoms, and each O₂ supplies two.

misconceptions.feedback: One O₂ supplies two O atoms, but the CO₂ and the waters need more.
That is the number of O atoms needed. Each O₂ supplies two of them.

questions.prompt: What may you change while balancing a fixed chemical reaction?
hints: Preserve every substance's formula.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Coefficients adjust quantities without changing substances.

questions.onCorrect: Coefficients change the quantity of each substance. Changing a subscript would change the substance.

misconceptions.feedback: A subscript is part of the formula. Change it and you have a different substance.
An element's identity cannot be changed by a reaction.

questions.prompt: Balance N₂ + ? H₂ → 2 NH₃. What coefficient belongs before H₂?
hints: Each H₂ provides two hydrogen atoms.
Two ammonias have six H atoms altogether.
Divide six H atoms by two per H₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two NH₃ molecules contain six H atoms, supplied by three H₂.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Two NH₃ hold six H atoms, and each H₂ supplies two.

misconceptions.feedback: Two H₂ supply four H atoms, but the ammonia needs more.
That is the number of H atoms needed. Each H₂ supplies two of them.

questions.prompt: Balance 2 Mg + O₂ → ? MgO. What coefficient belongs before MgO?
hints: Count each element separately.
Each MgO contains one Mg and one O.
Match both given magnesium atoms with one MgO unit each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two MgO formula units preserve both Mg atoms and both O atoms.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The left has two Mg atoms and two O atoms, so two MgO units match both.

misconceptions.feedback: One MgO holds one Mg, but the left has more Mg atoms than that.

questions.prompt: What must a balanced equation conserve?
hints: Compare element counts rather than total molecules.

acceptedIdeas: The count of each element's atoms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms rearrange; the number of molecules may change.

choices.label: The number of molecules on each side
The count of each element's atoms
The volume of every gas separately

questions.onCorrect: Atoms are conserved, so every element's count matches on both sides. The number of molecules can change.

misconceptions.feedback: Molecules can combine or split. It is the atoms that are conserved.
Equations balance atoms, not gas volumes.

questions.prompt: How many packs of wheels do you need?
hints: How many wheels do 3 cars need in total?
Each pack holds the same number of wheels.
Divide the wheels needed by the wheels in a pack.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Work out what you need, then how many of the pack supplies it. Balancing an equation asks the same thing of atoms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of wheels. The wheels come in packs.
That is the number of cars. Count the wheels first.

questions.prompt: In 2 Li + F₂ → 2 LiF, how many F atoms are on the right-hand side?
hints: The number in front multiplies the whole formula.
How many F atoms are in one LiF?
Multiply the coefficient by the F atoms in one unit.
questions.onCorrect: 2. The coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the F in one LiF. The coefficient multiplies it.
That counts the Li atoms as well. The question asks about F.

questions.prompt: Why must we not change KCl to K₂Cl to balance?

acceptedIdeas: Changing a subscript makes a different substance, so only coefficients may change

choices.label: Changing a subscript makes a different substance, so only coefficients may change
Subscripts are always correct in any compound
K₂Cl would have too many chlorine atoms

questions.onCorrect: Right: the formula names the substance, and only coefficients change how much of it there is.

misconceptions.feedback: Subscripts come from the substance, which is why we do not edit them to balance.
The issue is not the number of atoms. K₂Cl is simply not the substance we started with.

questions.prompt: Balance ? Al + 3 Cl₂ → 2 AlCl₃. What coefficient belongs before Al?
hints: Count the Al atoms in the product.
Each AlCl₃ holds one Al.
Match the Al atoms on the left to the right.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 AlCl₃ hold 2 Al, so the left needs 2 Al.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The product has two Al atoms, so the left needs two.

misconceptions.feedback: One Al would give one Al atom, but the product has more.
That is the coefficient of Cl₂. Match the aluminium atoms.

questions.prompt: Balance 2 C₂H₆ + ? O₂ → 4 CO₂ + 6 H₂O. What coefficient belongs before O₂?
hints: Count the O atoms in 4 CO₂.
Add the O atoms in 6 H₂O.
Divide the total O atoms by the atoms in one O₂.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The products hold 14 O atoms, and each O₂ supplies two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of O atoms needed. Each O₂ supplies two of them.
That counts only the oxygen in the CO₂. The waters hold oxygen too.
